1. Consider two proteins P and Q with identical native structures. By O1, the native structure of each corresponds to the global minimum of its respective free energy landscape. Since the structures are identical, their global minima correspond to the same spatial conformation. [O1]

2. For protein P, the TM-score between its native structure and itself is 1 by T1. Similarly, for protein Q, the TM-score between its native structure and itself is 1 by T1. [T1]

3. Now consider comparing the native structure of P to a different reference structure R (which is not the native structure of P). The TM-score formula from O4 is TM-score = max[ (1/L_target) Σ_i 1/(1+(d_i/d_0(L_target))^2) ], where L_target is the length of the target protein (here, P). [O4]

4. Similarly, consider comparing the native structure of Q to the same reference structure R. The TM-score formula applies with L_target being the length of Q. [O4]

5. If the lengths of P and Q differ, then L_target in the two calculations differs. The denominator d_0(L_target) in the TM-score formula depends on L_target (typically d_0(L) ≈ 1.24 * ∛(L - 15) for standard normalization). Therefore, the scaling factor d_0(L_target) is different for the two comparisons. [O4]

6. Consequently, the sum Σ_i 1/(1+(d_i/d_0(L_target))^2) will be scaled differently when divided by L_target, and the maximum over alignments may also be affected by the length-dependent normalization. Thus, the resulting TM-scores for P vs R and Q vs R can differ. [O4]

7. Therefore, for two proteins with identical native structures, their TM-scores to themselves are both 1, but their TM-scores to other reference structures may differ if their lengths differ. This completes the argument. [O1,T1,O4]

1. Consider two proteins P and Q with identical native structures. By O1, the native structure of each corresponds to the global minimum of its respective free energy landscape. Since the structures are identical, their global minima correspond to the same spatial conformation. [O1]

2. For protein P, the TM-score between its native structure and itself is 1 by T1. Similarly, for protein Q, the TM-score between its native structure and itself is 1 by T1. [T1]

3. Now consider comparing the native structure of P to a different reference structure R (which is not the native structure of P). The TM-score formula from O4 is TM-score = max[ (1/L_target) Σ_i 1/(1+(d_i/d_0(L_target))^2) ], where L_target is the length of the target protein (here, P). [O4]

4. Similarly, consider comparing the native structure of Q to the same reference structure R. The TM-score formula applies with L_target being the length of Q. [O4]

5. If the lengths of P and Q differ, then L_target in the two calculations differs. The denominator d_0(L_target) in the TM-score formula depends on L_target (typically d_0(L) ≈ 1.24 * ∛(L - 15) for standard normalization). Therefore, the scaling factor d_0(L_target) is different for the two comparisons. [O4]

6. Consequently, the sum Σ_i 1/(1+(d_i/d_0(L_target))^2) will be scaled differently when divided by L_target, and the maximum over alignments may also be affected by the length-dependent normalization. Thus, the resulting TM-scores for P vs R and Q vs R can differ. [O4]

7. Therefore, for two proteins with identical native structures, their TM-scores to themselves are both 1, but their TM-scores to other reference structures may differ if their lengths differ. This completes the argument. [O1,T1,O4]
